title: The Global Water Crisis: Why We're Running Out

lines: Clean water from a tap seems endless.
But controlling water has shaped civilization.
Today, 7 in 10 people have running water.
Yet many cities face critical shortages.
Water access remains unequal worldwide.
slides.keyIdea: Access to clean water has been central to human civilization, but today many major cities face severe water shortages.

lines: Cape Town nearly ran out of water.
Four million people faced water rationing.
Ten major cities will face similar crises.
By 2040, most regions lack year-round water.
We're at a critical inflection point.
slides.keyIdea: Multiple major cities worldwide are approaching water crises within the next few decades unless consumption changes dramatically.

lines: Earth has 326 million trillion gallons.
But 97% is salty, 2% is frozen.
Humans rely on just 1% of water.
Water access depends on geography.
Canada has 10,000 times more than Kuwait.
slides.keyIdea: Although Earth has abundant water, only 1% is freshwater accessible to humans, and distribution is extremely unequal.

lines: Mexico City drained its lakes centuries ago.
Population exploded to 22 million people.
Now the city pumps groundwater unsustainably.
Half the water supply will vanish in 30-50 years.
Extracting groundwater causes the city to sink.
slides.keyIdea: Mexico City's unsustainable groundwater extraction will deplete its water supply within decades while causing the city to physically sink.

lines: Water consumption increased sevenfold this century.
Personal use is only 8% of freshwater.
Agriculture and industry use the rest.
One hamburger requires 1,650 liters of water.
Global meat consumption keeps rising unsustainably.
slides.keyIdea: Most freshwater goes to agriculture and industry, especially meat production, which is increasingly unsustainable as global consumption rises.

lines: Water is priced as if it's unlimited.
Farmers pay almost nothing for water.
Southern California grows alfalfa in deserts.
Mexico City loses half its water to leaks.
We dump 2 million tons of waste daily.
slides.keyIdea: Water is underpriced globally, leading to wasteful agricultural practices, poor infrastructure maintenance, and pollution.

lines: Mexicali's brewery deal sparked fierce protests.
Water scarcity drives violent global conflicts.
Lake Chad drying caused livelihoods to collapse.
Darfur conflict linked to water scarcity.
Syrian drought may have triggered civil war.
slides.keyIdea: Water scarcity increasingly triggers violent conflicts and social unrest as governments prioritize industrial projects over agricultural and human needs.

lines: Cape Town cut water use in half through conservation.
Day Zero was postponed indefinitely by action.
Higher water prices hurt the poor most.
Philadelphia ties water prices to income.
Recognizing water's value can inspire change.
slides.keyIdea: Individual and collective action can address water crises, but solutions must balance conservation with protecting access as a human right.
